question: According to the passage, why had Biscuit been at the Maplewood Animal Shelter for almost four months without being adopted?

options.A: He was recovering from an injury that required ongoing medical treatment.
options.B: The shelter staff believed he was not yet ready to be adopted safely.
options.C: He was fearful around people and had not attracted serious adoption interest.
options.D: His previous family had specifically requested that he not be placed for adoption.

explanation: The correct answer is C (he was fearful around people and had not attracted serious adoption interest): the passage describes him pressing against the kennel wall and avoiding eye contact, directly connecting his fearful behaviour to the lack of adoption interest. Option A is never mentioned anywhere in the passage. Options B and D invent reasons that the passage never actually gives.
cluster_text:
When my mom suggested I volunteer at the Maplewood Animal Shelter over winter break instead of spending the entire two weeks watching videos in my room, I agreed mostly because I was bored, not because I particularly loved animals. I had never owned a pet, since our apartment building did not allow them, and I assumed volunteering would mostly involve cute, friendly dogs that wanted to be petted constantly.

Most of the dogs at the shelter were exactly like that, tails wagging the moment anyone walked past their kennel. Biscuit was different. He was a medium sized brown dog who pressed himself against the back wall of his kennel whenever a volunteer approached, refusing to make eye contact with anyone. The shelter staff told me he had been surrendered by a family that could no longer keep him, and that he had been there for almost four months without anyone showing serious interest in adopting him.

On my second day, I was assigned to sit quietly near Biscuit's kennel for fifteen minutes without trying to touch him or coax him toward me. It felt strange and a little pointless at first, just sitting on the cold concrete floor reading a book out loud to a dog that would not even look at me. The shelter coordinator, Mr. Ferreira, explained that some dogs need to learn that a person's presence does not automatically mean something bad is about to happen, and that trust sometimes has to be earned slowly, without any pressure at all.

I kept doing this every day for the rest of the week, reading whatever book I happened to be carrying, never expecting Biscuit to react differently. On my sixth visit, without any warning, he crept forward and rested his head near the edge of the kennel closest to where I sat, still not quite touching me, but noticeably closer than before. I did not move or make a sound, afraid that any sudden reaction might undo whatever small progress had just happened.

By the end of the two weeks, Biscuit would walk over and sit beside the kennel door whenever he heard my voice in the hallway, though he still flinched at loud noises and unfamiliar visitors. Mr. Ferreira told me that the quiet, patient time I had spent with him mattered more than any of the more obviously exciting tasks around the shelter, like walking the friendlier dogs or cleaning kennels.

I found out in February, almost a month after winter break ended, that a family had adopted Biscuit. Mr. Ferreira mentioned that they specifically noted he seemed comfortable with quiet visitors who did not rush him. I like to think that the fifteen minutes I spent sitting on cold concrete, reading books out loud to a dog who would not look at me, had something to do with that.

question: What can the reader infer about why Mr. Ferreira assigned Sofia to sit quietly near Biscuit's kennel without trying to touch him?

options.A: He needed volunteers to keep the shelter's noise level low during business hours.
options.B: He was testing whether Sofia was patient enough to continue volunteering long term.
options.C: He wanted to save the friendlier dogs for volunteers with more shelter experience.
options.D: He believed Biscuit needed to build trust gradually without feeling any pressure.

explanation: The correct answer is D (he believed Biscuit needed to build trust gradually without feeling any pressure): Mr. Ferreira explains this idea directly, saying some dogs need to learn that a person's presence is not automatically threatening. Option A is never suggested anywhere in the passage. Options B and C introduce reasons about testing volunteers or protecting other dogs that the passage never actually mentions.

question: According to the passage, what was the theme of the Youth Perspectives photography contest that year?

options.A: Community events that brought large groups of people together.
options.B: The simple, broad theme of belonging, open to any interpretation.
options.C: Family traditions passed down across multiple generations specifically.
options.D: Everyday objects that hold unexpected personal or emotional meaning.

explanation: The correct answer is B (the simple, broad theme of belonging, open to any interpretation): the passage states directly that the theme that year was simply belonging. Option A describes only one example idea other students chose, not the actual theme itself. Options C and D describe ideas related to Leah's own photo, not the official contest theme.
cluster_text:
I joined the photography club at Eastview High mostly because my schedule had an empty spot during lunch on Wednesdays and my friend Priya said the club always had good snacks. I had a decent phone camera and had taken plenty of pictures of sunsets and my cat, but I had never thought of photography as something I could actually be good at, let alone something worth entering into a contest.

Mr. Okafor, who ran the club, announced in October that the school board was holding its annual Youth Perspectives photography contest, open to any student willing to submit a single photo along with a short paragraph explaining its meaning. The theme that year was simply belonging. Several members of the club immediately started planning elaborate shots involving group friendships or big community events, the kind of images that obviously matched the theme.

I could not think of anything that felt right. Every idea I had seemed like something someone else would already be submitting. For almost three weeks, my camera roll stayed mostly empty except for the usual sunsets. Priya suggested I stop trying to think of the perfect concept and instead just start taking pictures of ordinary moments from my actual life, trusting that meaning would show up on its own rather than being forced.

One evening in early November, I photographed my grandmother's hands while she taught me to knead dough for bread, the same recipe she had learned from her own mother decades earlier in a kitchen thousands of kilometres from ours. I had not been thinking about the contest at all when I took the picture. It was only afterward, looking at the photo on my phone, that I realized it captured something about belonging that felt more honest than any staged group photo could have.

I almost did not submit it, worried that a close up photo of flour covered hands would seem too small or too personal compared to the ambitious ideas other students had described. Priya convinced me to submit it anyway, along with a short paragraph about how the recipe connected three generations of women in my family across different countries and decades.

When the contest results were announced in December, my photo was selected as one of ten finalists displayed in the front hallway of the school for an entire month. Strangers I did not know stopped to read the paragraph beside my photo, and a few even told me it reminded them of their own grandparents. I did not win first place, but standing in that hallway watching people connect with something so personal to my own family taught me that the smallest, quietest moments sometimes carry the most meaning, if you are willing to actually look for them.

Every afternoon for three weeks, I pushed my skateboard up the ramp at Cedarbrook Skatepark and tried the same trick: a simple kickflip. Every afternoon, I landed on my hip instead of my wheels. My older brother, Malik, sat on the bench nearby, watching without saying much, which somehow made the failures feel louder.

The park was busiest around four o'clock, right after the middle school let out, so I usually had an audience of at least a dozen kids whether I wanted one or not. That Thursday, a group of younger skaters had gathered near the quarter pipe, and I could feel their eyes on me as I set up for another attempt. My hands were sweating even though the October air was cool.

I pushed off, flicked my foot the way I had watched a hundred videos explain, and the board spun beneath me exactly like it was supposed to. For half a second, I actually believed I had done it. Then my back foot missed the tail, and I crashed sideways onto the concrete, scraping my palm badly enough that it started to bleed almost right away.

A couple of the younger kids laughed, not unkindly, just the way people laugh when someone falls down in a cartoon. I wanted to grab my board and walk straight to the bus stop and never come back. Instead, I sat on the ground for a second longer than I needed to, mostly because my hip hurt and partly because I didn't trust my legs yet.

Malik walked over, not fast, and crouched down next to me. He didn't ask if I was okay, which I appreciated, because obviously I wasn't fully okay. Instead he said, 'You know how many times I ate concrete before I landed my first ollie? You weren't even born yet, and I was still falling.' I laughed despite myself, and it stung my scraped hand a little.

'Everyone here has watched somebody wipe out,' he added, nodding toward the group of younger kids, who had already moved on to their own tricks and weren't paying attention to me anymore. 'Nobody remembers the fall. They remember whether you got back up.'

I wrapped a tissue around my palm, grabbed my board, and rolled back toward the ramp. My legs were shaking, and I still felt the ghost of every kid's laughter, but underneath that there was something steadier taking hold. I set up for the kickflip one more time. I didn't land it that day either, not once, but on my sixth try I stayed on my feet for a full second longer than before, and that felt like enough.

By the time Malik and I walked home as the streetlights came on, my hand had stopped bleeding and my hip had stopped complaining quite so much. I hadn't landed the trick I came for, but I had figured out something more useful: the fear of falling in front of people had been bigger in my head than it ever was at the actual skatepark.

Every afternoon for three weeks, I pushed my skateboard up the ramp at Cedarbrook Skatepark and tried the same trick: a simple kickflip. Every afternoon, I landed on my hip instead of my wheels. My older brother, Malik, sat on the bench nearby, watching without saying much, which somehow made the failures feel louder.

The park was busiest around four o'clock, right after the middle school let out, so I usually had an audience of at least a dozen kids whether I wanted one or not. That Thursday, a group of younger skaters had gathered near the quarter pipe, and I could feel their eyes on me as I set up for another attempt. My hands were sweating even though the October air was cool.

I pushed off, flicked my foot the way I had watched a hundred videos explain, and the board spun beneath me exactly like it was supposed to. For half a second, I actually believed I had done it. Then my back foot missed the tail, and I crashed sideways onto the concrete, scraping my palm badly enough that it started to bleed almost right away.

A couple of the younger kids laughed, not unkindly, just the way people laugh when someone falls down in a cartoon. I wanted to grab my board and walk straight to the bus stop and never come back. Instead, I sat on the ground for a second longer than I needed to, mostly because my hip hurt and partly because I didn't trust my legs yet.

Malik walked over, not fast, and crouched down next to me. He didn't ask if I was okay, which I appreciated, because obviously I wasn't fully okay. Instead he said, 'You know how many times I ate concrete before I landed my first ollie? You weren't even born yet, and I was still falling.' I laughed despite myself, and it stung my scraped hand a little.

'Everyone here has watched somebody wipe out,' he added, nodding toward the group of younger kids, who had already moved on to their own tricks and weren't paying attention to me anymore. 'Nobody remembers the fall. They remember whether you got back up.'

I wrapped a tissue around my palm, grabbed my board, and rolled back toward the ramp. My legs were shaking, and I still felt the ghost of every kid's laughter, but underneath that there was something steadier taking hold. I set up for the kickflip one more time. I didn't land it that day either, not once, but on my sixth try I stayed on my feet for a full second longer than before, and that felt like enough.

By the time Malik and I walked home as the streetlights came on, my hand had stopped bleeding and my hip had stopped complaining quite so much. I hadn't landed the trick I came for, but I had figured out something more useful: the fear of falling in front of people had been bigger in my head than it ever was at the actual skatepark.

It was late October, already getting dark by six, and I had only gone down to the ravine because my mom had sent me to look for our cat, who turned out to be sitting on our own back porch the entire time.

Up close, it looked thin, its ribs slightly visible beneath its matted fur, and I guessed it had probably been out here for at least a few days.

I didn't have a leash, so I ended up using the drawstring from my hoodie, looping it gently around the dog's neck while talking to it in the calmest voice I could manage, even though my own heart was pounding. The walk home took twice as long as usual because the dog kept stopping to sniff every third fence post, and I kept glancing over my shoulder half expecting someone to come running after us claiming it was theirs.

My mom was not thrilled when I showed up with a strange, limping dog instead of our cat, but she softened once she saw how gently it leaned against my leg on the porch. I posted photos on three different community boards, and on the third night, I got a message from a woman named Renata who lived across the ravine and had lost her dog, Toffee, nine days earlier after a thunderstorm spooked him out of her backyard.

When Renata arrived the next afternoon, Toffee, or Biscuit, or whatever his real name was in that moment, went completely still for a second and then practically threw himself against her legs, his tail moving so fast it was almost a blur. After she left with Toffee trotting happily beside her, our laundry room felt strangely empty for a few days. I hadn't planned on getting attached to a dog I only had for four days, but I found myself checking the community board out of habit anyway, just in case somebody else's pet needed finding.

cluster_text:
When my dad's back injury put him on strict bed rest for three weeks, somebody had to start cooking dinner, and since my older sister was away at a volleyball tournament that first week, that somebody turned out to be me. Before that, my cooking experience mostly involved reheating leftovers and making toast, so the idea of preparing an actual meal for four people felt genuinely overwhelming.

The first night, I attempted spaghetti because it seemed like the simplest possible option, and I still managed to overcook the noodles into something closer to paste while somehow undercooking the sauce, leaving it watery and bland. My mom, exhausted from working a full day and then checking on my dad every hour, ate it anyway without complaining, though my younger brother made a face he clearly thought was subtle.

I called my grandmother that night, mostly out of desperation, and she talked me through some basic timing mistakes over speakerphone while I stood in the kitchen with a notepad. She reminded me that pasta keeps cooking a little even after you drain it, and that sauce needs time to actually reduce and thicken rather than being dumped on immediately. It sounded obvious once she explained it, though it clearly hadn't been obvious to me an hour earlier.

Over the following two weeks, I worked my way through a short list of dishes my grandmother walked me through one at a time: a simple stir fry, baked chicken with vegetables, a lentil soup that took nearly two hours but mostly just sat on the stove without needing much attention from me. Some nights went fine. One memorable Wednesday, I nearly set off the smoke alarm trying to fry rice at too high a heat, and my dad, forbidden from getting out of bed, shouted cooking advice down the hallway that I could barely understand.

By the middle of the third week, dinner had stopped feeling like a crisis I was barely surviving and started feeling like an actual task I could handle, even if it wasn't always exciting. My mom mentioned one evening, almost offhand, that the lentil soup was better than the version she usually made, which surprised me enough that I made her repeat it.

When my dad was finally cleared to stand in the kitchen again, though still not allowed to lift anything heavy, he asked me to make the stir fry so he could watch how I did it, correcting my knife grip but otherwise mostly just observing. Afterward he admitted he hadn't expected me to actually stick with cooking dinner every night rather than just ordering food or reheating something from the freezer.

Looking back at those three weeks now, I don't think I became some kind of skilled cook overnight, but I stopped being someone who was afraid of the kitchen, which felt like its own kind of accomplishment by the time my dad was finally back on his feet.

I had circled the date on my calendar three weeks before basketball tryouts even started. Every afternoon after school, I dribbled a ball around our driveway until the streetlights came on, practicing crossovers I had watched a hundred times online. My older brother, Malcolm, used to play for our school, and I wanted nothing more than to wear the same navy jersey he once wore.

On the first day of tryouts, the gym felt smaller than I remembered, packed with almost forty kids all fighting for twelve spots. Coach Reyes blew her whistle and split us into groups for layup drills. My hands were sweating so badly that I fumbled the ball twice before I even took a shot. I could feel my face turning red as a few of the older kids snickered behind me.

By the second drill, a full-court scrimmage, I had settled down enough to make a few decent passes, but I missed an easy shot under the basket that would have tied the score for my team. Coach Reyes didn't yell. She just wrote something on her clipboard and moved on to watch the next group. I spent the whole bus ride home replaying that missed shot over and over, certain I had blown my only chance.

When the list of names went up on the gym door two days later, I scanned it three times before I finally accepted that mine wasn't there. I didn't make the team. I stood in the hallway holding my backpack, trying to figure out how I would explain this to Malcolm, when Coach Reyes came out of her office and asked me to wait a moment.

She told me something I hadn't expected. She said she remembered exactly which drill I had struggled with, not because I was bad, but because of what I did right after missing that shot. Instead of sulking, I had sprinted back on defence and stolen the ball from the other team. She said that kind of hustle is harder to teach than shooting, and she invited me to join the junior practice squad that trains with the main team twice a week, even though I wouldn't be dressing for games yet.

I almost said no. Practicing without ever playing in a real game sounded like a consolation prize, and part of me wanted to just quit and try out for something else next year. But then I thought about how much I actually loved being in that gym, the squeak of sneakers on the floor and the sound of the ball hitting the rim. I told Coach Reyes I would be there Monday.

Three months later, one of the starting guards sprained his ankle right before the biggest game of the season. Coach Reyes called my name off the bench in the third quarter. My legs were shaking as I ran onto the court, but I remembered exactly what she had told me in that hallway. I didn't need to be the best shooter in the gym. I just needed to give everything I had to every single play. We won that game by four points, and afterward Malcolm told me it was the proudest he had ever been of me. I still think about that missed shot sometimes, and how close I came to walking away before I ever got the chance to prove what I could do.

I had circled the date on my calendar three weeks before basketball tryouts even started. Every afternoon after school, I dribbled a ball around our driveway until the streetlights came on, practicing crossovers I had watched a hundred times online. My older brother, Malcolm, used to play for our school, and I wanted nothing more than to wear the same navy jersey he once wore.

On the first day of tryouts, the gym felt smaller than I remembered, packed with almost forty kids all fighting for twelve spots. Coach Reyes blew her whistle and split us into groups for layup drills. My hands were sweating so badly that I fumbled the ball twice before I even took a shot. I could feel my face turning red as a few of the older kids snickered behind me.

By the second drill, a full-court scrimmage, I had settled down enough to make a few decent passes, but I missed an easy shot under the basket that would have tied the score for my team. Coach Reyes didn't yell. She just wrote something on her clipboard and moved on to watch the next group. I spent the whole bus ride home replaying that missed shot over and over, certain I had blown my only chance.

When the list of names went up on the gym door two days later, I scanned it three times before I finally accepted that mine wasn't there. I didn't make the team. I stood in the hallway holding my backpack, trying to figure out how I would explain this to Malcolm, when Coach Reyes came out of her office and asked me to wait a moment.

She told me something I hadn't expected. She said she remembered exactly which drill I had struggled with, not because I was bad, but because of what I did right after missing that shot. Instead of sulking, I had sprinted back on defence and stolen the ball from the other team. She said that kind of hustle is harder to teach than shooting, and she invited me to join the junior practice squad that trains with the main team twice a week, even though I wouldn't be dressing for games yet.

I almost said no. Practicing without ever playing in a real game sounded like a consolation prize, and part of me wanted to just quit and try out for something else next year. But then I thought about how much I actually loved being in that gym, the squeak of sneakers on the floor and the sound of the ball hitting the rim. I told Coach Reyes I would be there Monday.

I just needed to give everything I had to every single play. We won that game by four points, and afterward Malcolm told me it was the proudest he had ever been of me. I still think about that missed shot sometimes, and how close I came to walking away before I ever got the chance to prove what I could do.

The bell above the door of Sunrise Bakery jingled every time a customer walked in, and by my third shift I still hadn't gotten used to how loud it sounded compared to the quiet of my own kitchen at home. I had begged my parents for weeks to let me get a part-time job, mostly because I wanted to save up for a new bike, and Sunrise Bakery was the only place within walking distance that was hiring someone my age.

My manager, Mrs. Okafor, had trained me on the register during my first two shifts, but she still stood beside me most mornings just in case. On the third Saturday, she finally stepped away to help in the kitchen, telling me I was ready to handle the counter alone during the slower afternoon hours. I felt a mix of pride and nervousness as I watched her disappear behind the swinging door.

Everything went smoothly until a man in a business suit rushed in, glancing at his phone, and ordered two dozen assorted pastries for a meeting that apparently started in ten minutes. I grabbed boxes and started filling them as fast as I could, but I mixed up his order, giving him plain croissants instead of the almond ones he had specifically asked for. He didn't notice until he was already back at his office, and he called the bakery furious, demanding a refund and complaining loudly enough that Mrs. Okafor could hear his voice through the phone from across the counter.

I felt sick to my stomach as she hung up. I was certain I was about to be fired on the spot, and I started rehearsing an apology in my head before she even said anything. Instead, Mrs. Okafor asked me to walk her through exactly what had happened, step by step, without getting upset or making excuses. When I explained how rushed and flustered I had felt, she nodded and said that every new employee makes a mistake like this eventually, and that what mattered now was what I did next.

She had me personally box a fresh dozen almond croissants and deliver them to the man's office two blocks away, along with a handwritten note apologizing for the mix-up. My hands were shaking as I handed the box to his assistant, but I felt a strange sense of relief once it was done, like I had actually fixed something instead of just being scolded for breaking it.

The following week, that same man came back into the bakery, and I froze behind the register, bracing myself for another complaint. Instead, he said the croissants I had delivered were the best he had ever tasted and asked if I could recommend something for his daughter's birthday. I realized then that Mrs. Okafor hadn't just been protecting the bakery's reputation when she sent me to fix my mistake. She had been teaching me that owning up to an error and doing the work to correct it could turn even an angry customer into someone who trusted you again.

options.A: Whether Mrs. Okafor happened to be available to speak with him personally that day.
options.B: Whether the narrator could recommend something for his daughter's birthday.
options.C: Whether the bakery could deliver fresh pastries to his office every single week.
options.D: Whether the narrator still planned on continuing to work at Sunrise Bakery.

explanation: The correct answer is B (Whether the narrator could recommend something for his daughter's birthday): The passage states that the customer asked if the narrator could recommend something for his daughter's birthday. Option A is not mentioned, since he speaks directly to the narrator instead. Option C is never brought up anywhere in the passage. Option D is also not something the customer asks about during this scene.
cluster_text:
The bell above the door of Sunrise Bakery jingled every time a customer walked in, and by my third shift I still hadn't gotten used to how loud it sounded compared to the quiet of my own kitchen at home. I had begged my parents for weeks to let me get a part-time job, mostly because I wanted to save up for a new bike, and Sunrise Bakery was the only place within walking distance that was hiring someone my age.

My manager, Mrs. Okafor, had trained me on the register during my first two shifts, but she still stood beside me most mornings just in case. On the third Saturday, she finally stepped away to help in the kitchen, telling me I was ready to handle the counter alone during the slower afternoon hours. I felt a mix of pride and nervousness as I watched her disappear behind the swinging door.

Everything went smoothly until a man in a business suit rushed in, glancing at his phone, and ordered two dozen assorted pastries for a meeting that apparently started in ten minutes. I grabbed boxes and started filling them as fast as I could, but I mixed up his order, giving him plain croissants instead of the almond ones he had specifically asked for. He didn't notice until he was already back at his office, and he called the bakery furious, demanding a refund and complaining loudly enough that Mrs. Okafor could hear his voice through the phone from across the counter.

I felt sick to my stomach as she hung up. I was certain I was about to be fired on the spot, and I started rehearsing an apology in my head before she even said anything. Instead, Mrs. Okafor asked me to walk her through exactly what had happened, step by step, without getting upset or making excuses. When I explained how rushed and flustered I had felt, she nodded and said that every new employee makes a mistake like this eventually, and that what mattered now was what I did next.

She had me personally box a fresh dozen almond croissants and deliver them to the man's office two blocks away, along with a handwritten note apologizing for the mix-up. My hands were shaking as I handed the box to his assistant, but I felt a strange sense of relief once it was done, like I had actually fixed something instead of just being scolded for breaking it.

The following week, that same man came back into the bakery, and I froze behind the register, bracing myself for another complaint. Instead, he said the croissants I had delivered were the best he had ever tasted and asked if I could recommend something for his daughter's birthday. I realized then that Mrs. Okafor hadn't just been protecting the bakery's reputation when she sent me to fix my mistake. She had been teaching me that owning up to an error and doing the work to correct it could turn even an angry customer into someone who trusted you again.

question: According to the passage, what event in gaming history does the passage identify as an early root of esports?

options.A: The invention of home video game consoles for family use.
options.B: The launch of the first video streaming platform online.
options.C: The opening of the first Ontario varsity esports program.
options.D: Small arcade tournaments held in the 1980s.

explanation: The correct answer is D (Small arcade tournaments held in the 1980s): Small arcade tournaments held in the 1980s. The passage states this directly, describing players competing for high scores on games like Space Invaders. Options A, B, and C describe developments the passage mentions later or not at all, not the earliest root it identifies.
cluster_text:
Competitive video gaming, often called esports, has grown from a small hobby community into a major form of entertainment watched by millions of people worldwide. Esports involves organized video game competitions, often between professional teams, played in front of live audiences or streamed online to fans. Popular esports titles include team-based strategy games, first-person shooters, and sports simulations, each with its own professional leagues, sponsors, and dedicated fan base.

The roots of esports stretch back to small arcade tournaments held in the 1980s, where players competed for high scores on games like Space Invaders. For decades, competitive gaming remained a niche activity known mainly to dedicated fans. That changed dramatically with the rise of high-speed internet and video streaming platforms, which made it possible for anyone with an internet connection to watch top players compete in real time, no matter where in the world they lived. Today, major esports tournaments fill entire arenas and offer prize pools worth millions of dollars, rivaling some traditional professional sports events.

Ontario has become an active part of this growth. Several Ontario high schools and universities now offer varsity esports programs, complete with coaches, practice schedules, and scholarships for skilled players. Some school boards have added esports as an official extracurricular activity, treating it similarly to basketball or volleyball, with tryouts and structured team practices. Supporters argue that esports teaches teamwork, quick decision-making, and communication skills that transfer well to other areas of life, much like traditional team sports do.

Despite its growing acceptance, esports still faces questions that traditional sports rarely deal with. Concerns about excessive screen time, the physical strain of long practice sessions, and the pressure young players face to perform for an online audience are all topics that researchers and parents continue to debate. Some professional esports organizations have responded by hiring sports psychologists and physical trainers, treating player wellness as seriously as any traditional sports team would.

For many teens, esports offers an entry point into gaming as a possible career path, whether as a player, a broadcaster, a coach, or an event organizer. Post-secondary programs in game design, sports management, and digital broadcasting increasingly include esports-specific courses, reflecting how quickly the industry has grown. While not every young player will go on to compete professionally, the skills built through organized esports, including strategy, cooperation, and composure under pressure, can carry over into many other pursuits long after a person stops playing competitively.

question: According to the passage, what is a protected bike lane?

options.A: A lane reserved exclusively for buses and emergency vehicles, with no separation for cyclists at all.
options.B: A lane marked only with painted lines on the pavement while remaining fully shared with passing car traffic.
options.C: A bike lane physically separated from car traffic by a curb, planters, or posts.
options.D: A temporary lane installed only during major city festivals and removed again once the event has ended.

explanation: The correct answer is C (A bike lane physically separated from car traffic by a curb, planters, or posts): A bike lane physically separated from car traffic by a curb, planters, or posts. The passage defines a protected bike lane this way in its first paragraph. Options A, B, and D describe different features the passage does not attribute to protected bike lanes.
cluster_text:
Cities across Ontario have been adding dedicated bike lanes to major streets, aiming to give cyclists a safer, more predictable space to travel separate from car traffic. A bike lane is a section of roadway reserved specifically for bicycles, sometimes marked only with painted lines and sometimes physically separated from car traffic by a raised curb, planters, or flexible posts. City planners generally agree that physically separated bike lanes, often called protected bike lanes, provide a greater sense of safety for cyclists than lanes marked with paint alone.

The push for more bike lanes has grown alongside a broader effort by many municipalities to reduce car traffic, lower greenhouse gas emissions, and encourage residents to choose walking or cycling for short trips instead of driving. Traffic studies conducted in several Ontario cities have found that streets with protected bike lanes tend to see fewer serious collisions involving cyclists, since drivers and cyclists have clearly separated space rather than sharing a single lane.

Adding new bike lanes is rarely a simple process. City councils must weigh the benefits of improved cyclist safety against concerns raised by some residents and business owners, who worry that removing a lane of car traffic or on-street parking to make room for a bike lane could hurt local businesses or increase congestion for drivers. Public consultations, where residents can share their opinions before a project moves forward, have become a standard part of the process in most Ontario municipalities considering new bike infrastructure.

For teens who are old enough to cycle independently to school, part-time jobs, or friends' houses, protected bike lanes can make a real difference in whether a parent feels comfortable allowing that independence. A teen commuting along a busy arterial road without any bike lane must share space directly with fast-moving vehicles, while the same trip along a street with a protected bike lane offers a clearly marked, separated path. Several school boards have noted an increase in students cycling to school after nearby streets received new bike infrastructure, particularly on routes that previously required crossing multiple lanes of car traffic.

Despite ongoing debate over specific projects, most major Ontario cities have committed to long-term cycling network plans that aim to connect neighbourhoods with continuous, protected routes rather than short, disconnected segments. Transportation planners argue that a connected network matters more than any single lane, since a cyclist who feels safe on one street but must merge into traffic a block later gains little real benefit. As these networks slowly expand, city staff continue to track collision data and cyclist counts to determine which types of bike lanes work best in different neighbourhoods.

cluster_text:
Three-dimensional printing, often shortened to 3D printing, is a manufacturing process that builds solid objects layer by layer from a digital design. Unlike traditional manufacturing, which often starts with a large block of material and cuts away what is not needed, 3D printing adds material only where it is required, which is why the process is sometimes called additive manufacturing.

The process begins with a digital model created using computer-aided design software. This software allows a designer to build a three-dimensional shape on a screen, adjusting its size, angles, and internal structure before anything is physically produced. Once the design is finished, specialized slicing software converts the model into thin horizontal layers and generates precise instructions that tell the printer exactly where to place material for each layer.

Most 3D printers used in schools and homes rely on a method called fused deposition modelling. In this method, a spool of plastic filament is fed through a heated nozzle, which melts the plastic just enough to extrude it in a thin, controlled stream. The printer's nozzle moves back and forth across a build platform, tracing the outline of each layer according to the sliced instructions. Once one layer is complete, the platform lowers slightly, and the nozzle begins printing the next layer directly on top. This process repeats, sometimes for hours, until the final object is complete.

Other types of 3D printers use different materials and techniques. Some professional printers use a liquid resin that hardens when exposed to ultraviolet light, producing objects with a much smoother surface than filament-based printing can achieve. Industrial printers can even use powdered metal, fusing tiny particles together with a laser to create strong, precise parts used in fields such as aerospace and medicine.

3D printing has become useful across many industries because it allows designers to create prototypes quickly and cheaply compared to traditional manufacturing methods, which often require expensive moulds or tools before a single object can be produced. Engineers can test a design, identify flaws, and print a revised version within the same day rather than waiting weeks for a redesigned part to arrive.

Despite these advantages, 3D printing still has limitations. Printing large or highly detailed objects can take many hours, and the strength of a printed object depends heavily on the material used and how the layers are oriented. As the technology continues to improve, however, 3D printers are becoming faster, more affordable, and capable of working with an increasing variety of materials.

explanation: The correct answer is B (A pigment called chlorophyll that absorbs sunlight for photosynthesis): The passage states directly that leaves appear green because of chlorophyll, which absorbs sunlight to power photosynthesis. cluster_text:
Every autumn, the leaves on deciduous trees across Ontario shift from green to brilliant shades of yellow, orange, and red before eventually falling to the ground. While this seasonal change is often admired simply for its beauty, it is actually the result of a precise biological process that helps trees survive the colder months ahead.

During the spring and summer, leaves appear green because of a pigment called chlorophyll, which absorbs sunlight and uses its energy to convert water and carbon dioxide into sugars the tree can use for growth. This process, known as photosynthesis, requires warm temperatures and long hours of daylight to work efficiently. Chlorophyll is so abundant in a healthy leaf during these months that it masks other pigments that are present in the leaf the entire time.

As autumn approaches and daylight hours shorten, trees begin preparing for winter by shutting down photosynthesis in their leaves. A layer of specialized cells forms at the base of each leaf stem, gradually blocking the flow of water and nutrients between the leaf and the rest of the tree. Without a steady supply of resources, the leaf can no longer produce new chlorophyll, and the green pigment already present slowly breaks down.

As chlorophyll fades, other pigments that were hidden underneath become visible. Yellow and orange colours come from pigments called carotenoids, which are present in the leaf throughout the growing season but simply overshadowed by chlorophyll until autumn arrives. Red and purple colours, on the other hand, come from a different pigment called anthocyanin, which some trees actually produce in larger amounts during autumn, often triggered by bright sunny days combined with cool nights.

The exact colours and intensity of a given autumn vary from year to year depending on weather conditions. A growing season with plenty of rain followed by a dry, sunny autumn with cool but not freezing nights tends to produce the most vivid red and orange displays. In contrast, a fall with early frosts, heavy winds, or extended cloudy periods can cause leaves to turn brown and drop earlier without ever developing bright colours.

Eventually, the layer of cells at the base of the stem finishes sealing off the leaf completely, and it detaches from the branch. This process protects the tree from losing water through its leaves during winter, when frozen ground makes it difficult for roots to absorb moisture.

Recycling programs have become a standard part of daily life in Ontario schools, with colour-coded bins for paper, containers, and organic waste appearing in cafeterias, hallways, and classrooms across the province. While students often use these bins without thinking twice, the process of sorting and processing school waste involves several steps that most people never see.

Inside a typical school, recycling usually begins with three separate bins: one for paper and cardboard, one for plastic and metal containers, and one for organic waste such as food scraps and compostable packaging. Custodial staff or student volunteers empty these bins regularly, keeping the different materials separate so they do not become contaminated with items that do not belong. Contamination is a serious concern because a small amount of food waste mixed into a bin of paper can ruin an entire batch, forcing the whole bin to be sent to a landfill instead of a recycling facility.

Once collected, recyclable materials from a school are usually picked up by the same municipal waste service that serves nearby homes and businesses. At a materials recovery facility, machines and workers sort the mixed recyclables by material type, using magnets to pull out metal objects and optical scanners to separate different types of plastic. Paper and cardboard are baled into large blocks and shipped to mills, where they are broken down into pulp and turned into new paper products.

Organic waste follows a different path. Food scraps and compostable materials collected from schools are often sent to a composting facility, where they are combined with other organic waste and left to break down over several weeks or months. Workers monitor moisture and temperature levels throughout this process to speed up decomposition and prevent unpleasant odours. The finished compost is a nutrient-rich material that is often sold or given to farms, landscaping companies, or community gardens.

Many schools go beyond simply providing bins by running education programs that teach students how to sort waste correctly. Some schools appoint green teams of student volunteers who monitor bins during lunch periods, gently correcting classmates who place items in the wrong container. Research has shown that schools with active green teams tend to have significantly lower contamination rates than schools that rely on signage alone.

Even with these programs in place, recycling in schools is not perfect. Busy lunch periods, unclear labelling, and simple mistakes mean that some recyclable material still ends up in the garbage, which is why ongoing education remains an important part of any school recycling program.

cluster_text:
As concerns about climate change and rising energy costs continue to grow, solar panels have become an increasingly common sight on rooftops across Ontario. While most people know that solar panels somehow turn sunlight into electricity, the actual science behind the process involves a fascinating interaction between light and specially designed materials.

Solar panels are made up of many individual units called solar cells, most of which are constructed from a material called silicon. Silicon is a semiconductor, meaning it can control the flow of electricity better than a material like rubber, which blocks electricity entirely, but not as freely as a material like copper, which conducts electricity easily. This unique property makes silicon ideal for capturing and directing the energy carried by sunlight.

When sunlight strikes a solar cell, tiny packets of light energy called photons hit the silicon and transfer their energy to electrons within the material. This transfer of energy knocks the electrons loose, allowing them to move freely rather than staying fixed in place. Solar cells are specially designed with two layers of silicon that have been treated with different chemical elements, creating an internal electric field that pushes the loosened electrons in one consistent direction rather than letting them move randomly.

This organized movement of electrons creates an electric current, which flows out of the solar cell through metal contacts and wires. However, the electricity produced at this stage is direct current, the same type of electricity found in a battery, while most homes and the electrical grid run on alternating current. To solve this mismatch, solar panel systems include a device called an inverter, which converts the direct current produced by the panels into the alternating current that household appliances can actually use.

The amount of electricity a solar panel system produces depends on several factors, including the angle and direction the panels face, the amount of direct sunlight they receive throughout the day, and local weather conditions such as cloud cover. Panels installed on a south-facing roof in an area with long summer days typically generate significantly more electricity than panels installed in a shaded or poorly angled location.

Many homeowners who install solar panels also add a system for storing excess electricity in batteries or sending it back to the electrical grid, allowing them to use stored or credited energy during cloudy days or at night when their panels are not actively producing power.

Skateboarding has grown from a niche hobby into one of the most popular activities among Canadian teenagers, and many cities have responded by building dedicated skate parks. A skate park is a purpose-built space with ramps, rails, bowls, and ledges designed specifically for skateboarding, in-line skating, and BMX biking. Unlike skating on sidewalks or in parking lots, a skate park gives riders a controlled environment where they can practice tricks without worrying about traffic or angry store owners.

Building a skate park is not as simple as pouring a slab of concrete. City planners usually consult with local skateboarders before construction begins, asking which features riders actually want, such as a deep bowl for advanced skaters or a beginner-friendly area with gentle slopes. This kind of consultation has become common practice because early skate parks built without rider input often ended up unused, since the features did not match how people actually skated.

Safety remains one of the most debated topics surrounding skate parks. Studies of skateboarding injuries consistently show that wrist fractures and head injuries make up a large share of emergency room visits, and most of these injuries happen to beginners rather than experienced riders. Helmets, wrist guards, and knee pads dramatically reduce the severity of injuries, yet many teens skip this gear because they find it uncomfortable or believe it looks unfashionable among their peers.

Some skate parks have tried to encourage safety without seeming preachy about it. A few parks post friendly reminder signs at the entrance rather than strict rules, while others hold free clinics where local skate shop staff teach proper falling techniques alongside basic tricks. Falling correctly, by rolling instead of bracing with an outstretched arm, is one of the simplest ways to avoid a broken wrist, but it is a skill that takes deliberate practice to learn.

Beyond the physical benefits of exercise, skate parks often become informal social hubs. Teens who might not connect through school sports find a sense of belonging at the skate park, where skill level matters less than persistence and a willingness to keep trying after a fall. Many riders describe the atmosphere as more welcoming than competitive team sports, since skaters commonly cheer each other on even when they are strangers.

City officials continue to weigh the costs of maintaining these spaces against their popularity. A skate park requires regular inspection for cracked concrete and loose hardware, and vandalism or graffiti can add unexpected repair costs. Even so, most cities that have built skate parks report that ridership stays high year after year, suggesting the investment continues to pay off for the community.

In the last fifteen years, keeping honeybee hives on city rooftops has grown from an unusual hobby into a recognized part of urban agriculture in many Canadian cities. Rooftop apiaries, meaning collections of managed beehives, now sit above hotels, office buildings, and even some high schools, producing honey that is sold locally or used in school cooking programs. Supporters of urban beekeeping argue that cities actually offer bees a wider variety of flowering plants than rural areas dominated by a single crop, since gardens, parks, and boulevard trees bloom at different times throughout the season.

Bees play a role in the food system that most people rarely think about until it is explained to them. Many fruits and vegetables, including apples, blueberries, and squash, depend on pollinators to transfer pollen between flowers before they can produce fruit. Without enough bees visiting these plants, yields can drop noticeably, which is why some farms rent hives from beekeepers during the weeks their crops are in bloom rather than relying only on wild pollinators.

Concerns about declining bee populations have made this topic more urgent in recent years. Beekeepers have reported unusually high losses of entire hives over the winter months, a problem linked to several combined causes, including pesticide exposure, loss of wildflower habitat, and a parasitic mite that weakens colonies. While a single rooftop hive in a city will not reverse this broader trend on its own, beekeeping advocates argue that urban hives raise public awareness and encourage residents to plant more pollinator-friendly gardens.

Managing a hive safely in a crowded city setting requires careful planning that rural beekeepers rarely need to consider. options.B: It also reduces the need for quite as many school buses each morning
options.C: It is reportedly encouraged by provincial guidelines for most participating students
options.D: It is loosely associated with somewhat higher grades for students who regularly participate

explanation: The correct answer is A (It reduces the number of cars causing congestion during drop-off): The passage explains that school boards look to active transportation to reduce the number of cars dropping students off each morning, easing congestion near schools. Option B is never mentioned as a goal of these programs. Option C is also not supported anywhere in the passage. Option D likewise has no basis in the passage.
cluster_text:
Active transportation, a term used to describe any way of getting somewhere under your own power such as walking, cycling, or skateboarding, has become a focus for many Ontario school boards looking to reduce the number of cars dropping students off each morning. Streets near schools tend to become congested and occasionally dangerous during drop-off and pickup times, with parked cars blocking sightlines and drivers sometimes making quick, unsafe turns while trying to find a parking spot. Encouraging more students to walk or cycle is seen as one way to ease this daily traffic problem.

Cycling to school offers benefits that go beyond avoiding morning traffic. Regular physical activity before the school day begins has been linked to improved concentration in early morning classes, and some teachers report that students who arrive after a walk or bike ride seem more alert during first period than those who were driven directly from bed to the classroom door. For teens without easy access to a car or a ride, cycling can also provide a sense of independence that relying on a parent for transportation does not offer.

Safety concerns remain the most common reason parents hesitate to let their teens cycle to school, particularly on roads without dedicated bike lanes. Cities that have added protected bike lanes near schools, meaning lanes physically separated from car traffic by a curb or barrier, have generally seen cycling rates among students rise, since parents feel more confident their children are not sharing a lane directly with cars. Where no such infrastructure exists, some schools have organized bike trains instead, in which a group of students cycles together along a set route accompanied by a parent volunteer or staff member.

Weather and distance remain practical barriers that infrastructure alone cannot solve. A student who lives eight kilometres from school is unlikely to cycle there daily regardless of how safe the route is, and Ontario winters make cycling far less appealing for months at a time. Because of this, most active transportation programs focus on students who live within a reasonable distance, generally under three kilometres, and encourage cycling primarily during the milder months of the school year.

Bike storage at school is a smaller but still important piece of the puzzle. A school with only a handful of exposed bike racks near a busy entrance may discourage cycling simply because students worry about theft or vandalism, while covered, secure bike storage tends to see much higher use. Some schools have added bike repair stations with basic tools, allowing students to fix a loose chain or a flat tire without needing to walk the rest of the way.

Overall, school boards that have invested in active transportation programs report gradual rather than dramatic increases in cycling rates. Changing daily habits takes time, and a single new bike lane rarely transforms a neighbourhood's transportation patterns overnight. Even so, staff involved in these programs describe steady progress as worthwhile, arguing that every student who switches from being driven to cycling represents one less car in an already congested drop-off line.

Maplewood Robotics Team Heads to National Finals
By Priya Anand, Community News Reporter

MAPLEWOOD - A team of five Grade 10 students from Maplewood Secondary School earned a spot at the Canadian National Robotics Championship after their robot, nicknamed Ferris, took first place at last weekend's regional qualifier in Thunder Bay.

The team, called the Circuit Breakers, spent four months after school designing and building Ferris to complete a series of timed obstacle challenges, including sorting coloured blocks and climbing a small ramp. Out of eighteen teams at the regional event, Maplewood finished with the highest overall score, edging out a team from a much larger school in the final round.

"We rebuilt the arm mechanism three separate times before it finally worked the way we wanted," said team captain Malik Osei, age 15. "There were nights we thought about giving up, but our coach kept reminding us that engineers fail a lot before they succeed."

Coach and technology teacher Dana Fournier said the win reflects months of quiet, unglamorous problem-solving rather than a single lucky moment. "These students showed up every Tuesday and Thursday for four months," Fournier said. "What people see is the trophy, but what I saw was five kids learning to disagree respectfully and keep testing ideas until something worked."

The national championship will take place in Ottawa in six weeks, and the team is now fundraising to cover travel costs for its five members, one coach, and the equipment needed to transport Ferris safely. A bake sale held Tuesday raised just over four hundred dollars, and the school's parent council has pledged to match any additional donations up to one thousand dollars.

Community Food Drive Sets New Record, Organizers Say
By Sam Petrov, Northside Weekly

NORTHSIDE - This year's annual Northside Food Drive collected more than eighteen thousand pounds of food and household supplies, breaking the previous record by nearly four thousand pounds, organizers announced Monday.

The two-week drive, run each spring by a coalition of local schools and community groups, relies almost entirely on student volunteers who collect donations door to door and staff sorting stations at the community centre each evening.

"We set a goal of fifteen thousand pounds this year, and honestly I thought that was ambitious," said drive coordinator Michelle Tran. "When our final count came in, several of the student volunteers actually cheered."

Organizers credit the record total partly to a new competition between local high schools, which tracked donations by school and awarded a pizza party to the winning group. Eastwood Collegiate collected the most items overall, while Northside High School collected the most per student.

Grade 10 volunteer Devon Okafor spent four evenings sorting canned goods at the community centre. "It's easy to forget how much this stuff matters until you see how fast the shelves empty out again," Okafor said. "Some families come in the same week the food arrives."

Rosa Delgado, who manages the food bank that receives the donations, said demand has grown over the past two years and the drive's timing could not have been better. "Without events like this, we would be turning families away right now," Delgado said. "This drive alone will stock our shelves for close to two months."

Organizers are already planning next year's drive and hope to expand the school competition to include elementary schools for the first time. Tran said the coalition will meet this summer to review what worked well and to set a new fundraising goal for next spring.

"I must have taken that same shot maybe thirty times over two different mornings before I got the lighting right," Marchetti said. "My sister was not thrilled about waking up early for photos she didn't even ask for."

Contest judge Priya Anand, a professional photographer who reviewed all entries, said Marchetti's photo stood out because of what it left unglamorous rather than what it dressed up. "So many entries showed dramatic landscapes or posed portraits," Anand said. "This photo showed ordinary work at an ordinary hour, and that honesty is rare in a youth contest."

Marchetti said he originally entered the contest on a dare from a friend and almost withdrew the photo after seeing more polished entries from other schools during the submission period. His media teacher, Renata Kowalski, convinced him to leave it in.

"I told him the judges were looking for something true, not something perfect," Kowalski said. "Sometimes students think a contest wants the fanciest image, when really it wants the most honest one."

The win includes a five-hundred-dollar prize and a spot in a regional gallery exhibit opening next month, where Marchetti's photograph will hang alongside other winning entries from four school districts. Marchetti said he plans to give some of the prize money to his sister for waking up so early.

By Priya Nathan

GUELPH, ON — The Guelph Public Library announced this week that its downtown branch will stay open two hours later on weeknights throughout January, giving students extra quiet study space during exam season.

The extended hours, running until nine each weeknight instead of the usual seven o'clock closing, follow months of requests from local high school students who said the library often felt too crowded to find a seat during exam weeks.

"Before, I'd sometimes just go home because there wasn't anywhere to sit," Renner said. "Now I can actually plan to be here until closing without worrying I'll get kicked out early."

The extended hours are being funded through a temporary staffing budget approved by the city council specifically for the trial period. Fournier said the library will track how many students use the space during the extra hours before deciding whether to make the change permanent or expand it to other branches.

The Lakeside Wolves girls' soccer team secured a spot in the provincial semifinals on Sunday with a 2-1 win over the defending champions, a result few outside the team predicted at the start of the season. By Harriet Solaris, Northgate Ledger

A vacant lot on Birchwood Avenue that had sat empty for nearly a decade has been transformed into a thriving community garden, thanks to a partnership between local residents and a group of Northgate Secondary School students. The garden officially opened to the public on Saturday, featuring thirty raised planting beds available to families across the neighbourhood.

The project began last spring when a group of students in an environmental science class proposed turning the unused lot into a garden as part of a class assignment. What started as a school project quickly grew into a full community effort once neighbours got involved.

"We honestly thought we'd just write a report and move on," said grade eleven student Owen Kaminski, one of the project's original organizers. "Then our teacher suggested we actually pitch it to the city, and somehow here we are with real dirt under our fingernails."

The city agreed to lease the lot to the community group for five years at no cost, provided the garden remained open to any resident who wanted to grow food there. Local hardware stores donated soil, lumber for the raised beds, and gardening tools to get the project started.

Neighbourhood resident Consuela Reyes, who has lived on Birchwood Avenue for over twenty years, said she remembers when the lot was cleared for a housing development that never happened. "For years it was just an eyesore full of weeds," she said. "Now I walk by and see kids and grandparents working in the dirt together. It feels like the neighbourhood again."

Teacher Ms. Odalys Ferreira, who supervised the students throughout the project, said she was proud of how far the idea had travelled from its classroom origins. "They did the research, they made the pitch, and they kept showing up even when the city process moved slower than they expected," she said. "This is what happens when you take students seriously."

Organizers plan to host a fall harvest festival at the garden in October, with proceeds from a small produce sale going toward expanding the garden next year.

The garden officially opened to the public on Saturday, featuring thirty raised planting beds available to families across the neighbourhood.

The project began last spring when a group of students in an environmental science class proposed turning the unused lot into a garden as part of a class assignment. What started as a school project quickly grew into a full community effort once neighbours got involved.

"We honestly thought we'd just write a report and move on," said grade eleven student Owen Kaminski, one of the project's original organizers. "Then our teacher suggested we actually pitch it to the city, and somehow here we are with real dirt under our fingernails."

The city agreed to lease the lot to the community group for five years at no cost, provided the garden remained open to any resident who wanted to grow food there. Local hardware stores donated soil, lumber for the raised beds, and gardening tools to get the project started.

Neighbourhood resident Consuela Reyes, who has lived on Birchwood Avenue for over twenty years, said she remembers when the lot was cleared for a housing development that never happened. "For years it was just an eyesore full of weeds," she said. "Now I walk by and see kids and grandparents working in the dirt together. It feels like the neighbourhood again."

Teacher Ms. Odalys Ferreira, who supervised the students throughout the project, said she was proud of how far the idea had travelled from its classroom origins. "They did the research, they made the pitch, and they kept showing up even when the city process moved slower than they expected," she said. "This is what happens when you take students seriously."

Organizers plan to host a fall harvest festival at the garden in October, with proceeds from a small produce sale going toward expanding the garden next year.

question: Each sentence below should show that something belongs to a person or a group. Which of these sentences correctly use an apostrophe to show possession? Select all that apply.

options.A: The dog's leash was hanging by the front door all morning.
options.B: The dogs leash was hanging by the front door all morning.
options.C: The players' equipment was stored in the locker room overnight.
options.D: The players equipment was stored in the locker room overnight.
options.E: The team's uniforms were washed after every single game this season.

explanation: The correct answers are A, C, and E: A places the apostrophe before the s to show the leash belongs to one dog, C places the apostrophe after the s to show the equipment belongs to more than one player, and E places the apostrophe before the s to show the uniforms belong to the single team. Option B leaves out the apostrophe entirely, making dogs look like a plain plural noun instead of a possessive. Option D also leaves out the needed apostrophe before showing possession of the equipment.

question: Each pair of sentences below describes items that were left somewhere. Which of these sentences correctly match the pronoun in number with the noun it refers to? Select all that apply.

options.D: Wearing a bright helmet, the parked cars were passed quickly by the cyclist.

Option B places the modifier next to sunset, wrongly suggesting the sunset was riding along the trail. Option D places the modifier next to parked cars, wrongly suggesting the cars were wearing the helmet.

question: Each sentence below introduces a list of art supplies. Which of these sentences correctly use a colon to introduce the list? Select all that apply.

options.A: For art class, bring these supplies: a sketchbook, pencils, and an eraser.
options.B: For art class, bring these supplies, a sketchbook, pencils, and an eraser.
options.C: Pack the following items: a towel, sunscreen, and a reusable water bottle.
options.D: Pack the following items a towel, sunscreen, and a reusable water bottle.

explanation: The correct answers are A and C: both sentences correctly place a colon after a complete introductory clause, these supplies and the following items, right before the list of specific items begins. Option B uses a comma instead of a colon, which is less precise for introducing a list this way. Option D leaves out any punctuation before the list, making the sentence run together confusingly.

question: Each sentence below joins two complete ideas with a coordinating conjunction. Which of these sentences correctly place a comma before the coordinating conjunction? Select all that apply.

options.A: The field trip was rescheduled, but the weather forecast still looked promising.
options.B: The field trip was rescheduled but the weather forecast still looked promising.
options.C: The concert was cancelled, and the refunds were issued within a few days.
options.D: The concert was cancelled and the refunds were issued within a few days.

explanation: The correct answers are A and C: both sentences correctly place a comma right before the coordinating conjunction, but and and, since each one joins two complete, independent ideas. Option B leaves out the needed comma before but, joining the two complete ideas without proper punctuation. Option D also leaves out the needed comma before and.

question: The pronoun in the sentence below must be chosen correctly to match its role as the object of the sentence, describing who was invited to help. Which option correctly uses the object pronoun?

options.A: The teacher invited my friend and I to help set up the assembly.
options.B: The teacher invited my friend and myself to help set up the assembly.
options.C: The teacher invited my friend and me to help set up the assembly.
options.D: The teacher invited I and my friend to help set up the assembly.

explanation: The correct answer is C, "The teacher invited my friend and me to help set up the assembly": me is the correct object pronoun here, since the sentence describes who received the action of being invited, not who performed it. Option A incorrectly uses the subject pronoun I in an object position. Option B uses the reflexive pronoun myself, which is not appropriate since there is no matching subject I earlier in the sentence. Option D again places the subject pronoun I in an object position and awkwardly reorders the sentence.

question: Nobody could remember exactly ___ they had left their house keys before the trip.

options.A: where
options.B: were
options.C: we're
options.D: wear

explanation: The correct answer is A, "where": where asks about a location, which fits the sentence about not remembering a place the keys were left. Option B, were, is a past tense verb and does not fit the meaning of location needed here. Option C, we're, is a contraction of we are and does not make sense in this sentence. Option D, wear, refers to clothing or using something and has no connection to the intended meaning.

question: The first paragraph of an essay explains why school libraries are important for research skills. The second paragraph explains why libraries also matter for quiet study space. Which sentence would best transition between these two paragraphs?

options.A: Beyond helping students research effectively, libraries also provide a valuable quiet space to study.
options.B: Libraries have existed in schools for a very long time across many countries around the world.
options.C: Some students prefer studying at home rather than in a busy school library environment.
options.D: Research skills are taught in many different subjects throughout high school and beyond.

explanation: The correct answer is A, "Beyond helping students research effectively, libraries also provide a valuable quiet space to study": this sentence clearly connects the first paragraph's idea about research to the second paragraph's new idea about quiet study space, signalling the shift with beyond. Option B introduces an unrelated historical fact rather than linking the two specific ideas. Option C shifts to a new, contrasting idea about home study that does not bridge the two paragraphs. Option D repeats a detail from the first paragraph without introducing the second paragraph's new focus at all.

question: Which order below arranges these steps into the most logical process paragraph about baking chocolate chip cookies?

options.A: First, cream together the butter and sugar until the mixture is light and fluffy. Next, stir in the flour, baking soda, and chocolate chips until just combined. Then drop spoonfuls of dough onto a baking sheet, spacing them evenly apart. Finally, bake the cookies for about ten minutes until the edges turn golden brown.
options.B: Next, stir in the flour, baking soda, and chocolate chips until just combined. First, cream together the butter and sugar until the mixture is light and fluffy. Then drop spoonfuls of dough onto a baking sheet, spacing them evenly apart. Finally, bake the cookies for about ten minutes until the edges turn golden brown every time.
options.C: Then drop spoonfuls of dough onto a baking sheet, spacing them evenly apart. First, cream together the butter and sugar until the mixture is light and fluffy. Next, stir in the flour, baking soda, and chocolate chips until just combined. Finally, bake the cookies for about ten minutes until the edges turn golden brown every time.
options.D: First, cream together the butter and sugar until the mixture is light and fluffy. Next, stir in the flour, baking soda, and chocolate chips until just combined. Finally, bake the cookies for about ten minutes until the edges turn golden brown. Then drop spoonfuls of dough onto a baking sheet, spacing them evenly apart every time.

explanation: The correct answer is A, the order that creams the butter and sugar first, mixes in the dry ingredients, shapes the dough on the sheet, and bakes last: this follows the real baking process from start to finish. Option B mixes the dry ingredients before the butter and sugar have even been creamed together. Option C drops the dough onto the sheet before the dry ingredients have been mixed in at all. Option D places the baking step before the dough has actually been shaped and placed on the sheet.
items: Finally, bake the cookies for about ten minutes until the edges turn golden brown.
First, cream together the butter and sugar until the mixture is light and fluffy.
Next, stir in the flour, baking soda, and chocolate chips until just combined.
Then drop spoonfuls of dough onto a baking sheet, spacing them evenly apart.

question: Which order below arranges these sentences into the most logical paragraph describing Priya's closing shift at the bakery, from start to finish?

options.A: Priya arrived at the bakery at four o'clock to start her closing shift. Finally, she counted the register drawer and locked the front doors for the night. After clocking in, she wrapped the unsold pastries and placed them in the donation bin. Next, she wiped down the display cases and swept the floor before heading home.
options.B: Priya arrived at the bakery at four o'clock to start her closing shift. Next, she wiped down the display cases and swept the floor before heading home. After clocking in, she wrapped the unsold pastries and placed them in the donation bin. Finally, she counted the register drawer and locked the front doors for the night.

Next, she wiped down the display cases and swept the floor before heading home. Finally, she counted the register drawer and locked the front doors for the night.
options.D: After clocking in, she wrapped the unsold pastries and placed them in the donation bin. Priya arrived at the bakery at four o'clock to start her closing shift. Finally, she counted the register drawer and locked the front doors for the night. Next, she wiped down the display cases and swept the floor before heading home.

explanation: The correct answer is C (A, B, D, C: Priya arrived at the bakery at four o'clock to start her closing shift. After clocking in, she wrapped the unsold pastries and placed them in the donation bin. Next, she wiped down the display cases and swept the floor before heading home. Finally, she counted the register drawer and locked the front doors for the night.): This order follows the real sequence of a closing shift, arriving, handling leftover food, cleaning the space, and then securing the store last. items: Finally, she counted the register drawer and locked the front doors for the night.
Priya arrived at the bakery at four o'clock to start her closing shift.
